issues.legal_issue: Interest provided by the land-acquisition statute is not payable on rental compensation whose source is an executive order rather than the statute.
material_facts: The land was taken before the statutory acquisition notifications were issued.

The State’s executive resolutions provided for rental compensation when land was taken by private negotiation, but neither those resolutions nor the statute provided for interest on that rental compensation.
The High Court awarded interest by analogy with statutory interest provisions.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could not award interest on rental compensation by relying on statutory provisions governing interest on compensation under the Act, because the rental compensation arose from executive orders and was not an entitlement under the Act.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 17(3-A), 23(1-A), 28 and 34 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 govern statutory entitlements under that Act and do not extend by analogy to rental compensation created by executive orders. The Court did not rely on earlier cases in reaching this conclusion; Gadag Sub-Division, Gadag v. Mathapathi Basavannewwa and Executive Engineer, Irrigation Division v. Laghubhai Nanubhai were cited by the respondents.

predicates.land_acquisition_rental_compensation_dis: The dispute concerns rental compensation associated with land acquired by a public authority.
predicates.rental_compensation_created_by_executive: The public authority created the entitlement to rental compensation through an executive order rather than through the acquisition statute.
predicates.no_interest_entitlement_in_statute_or_or: Neither the applicable statute nor the executive order provides for interest on the rental compensation.

issues.definition: When a land-acquisition rental-compensation dispute concerns compensation created by executive order and neither the statute nor the order provides for interest, statutory interest is unavailable on that compensation.

issues.legal_issue: A public authority may not withhold rental compensation assessed by the acquisition officer merely because the final acquisition award remains under challenge or reference.
material_facts: The State had taken possession of the land and rental compensation was payable under its executive resolutions.
Rental compensation remained unpaid in many cases.
Some acquisition awards were still pending before a reference court or in appeal.
The Court considered that compensation calculated on the acquisition officer’s valuation could be paid and later adjusted if the valuation changed.
issues.conclusion: The pendency of a reference or appeal was not a legitimate excuse for withholding rental compensation calculated on the acquisition officer’s valuation; the compensation should be paid expeditiously, with any later variation adjusted as appropriate.
issues.legal_principle: An unresolved challenge to the acquisition award does not justify withholding an amount already calculable on the acquisition officer’s valuation. If the final valuation changes, the rental compensation can be recalculated and the amount paid adjusted. The Court relied on the State resolutions’ stated urgency in making payment, not on a statutory interest provision.

issues.legal_issue: Equity permits an award of interest on unpaid rental compensation despite the absence of a statutory entitlement to that interest.
material_facts: The State resolutions provided for rental compensation and emphasized prompt payment, but made no provision for interest.
Possession had been taken long before the landholders sought relief, and rental compensation remained unpaid in many cases without a legitimate excuse.
The writ applications were filed long after possession was taken, a circumstance the Court considered when working out the equities.
The Court excluded cases in which rental compensation had been paid before the commencement point it selected for interest.
issues.conclusion: The Court set aside the High Court’s statutory basis for interest but directed the State to pay interest at six per cent on unpaid rental compensation from 1 April 2000 until payment, excluding cases in which payment had already been made before that date.
issues.legal_principle: Although the Land Acquisition Act and the executive resolutions created no entitlement to interest on rental compensation, the Court could grant limited interest in equity where compensation was withheld without legitimate excuse. In shaping that relief, it considered the resolutions’ emphasis on prompt payment, the delay in seeking relief, and whether payment had already been made. The Court did not rely on an earlier case for this equitable direction.
